description:
We are a team of curious and creative young minds who love programming, technology, and exploring new ideas. We are excited to learn more about space and discover how technology and AI can help us explore the universe.

We are looking for enthusiastic, creative, and hardworking team members who are interested in programming, problem-solving, space science, and teamwork.

Join us, share your ideas, and let's turn our curiosity into amazing discoveries!
summary:
ORBITFORGE — Forge real space missions from NASA's open data.
 three connected pillars:
🎓 LEARN — A Rocket Builder academy where kids build a real rocket step-by-step against real NASA standards: the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, thrust-to-weight ≥ 1.2, staging, mass fractions — then fly it to orbit, the Moon, or Mars with real mission-leg physics, discovering that Mars landings are cheaper because aerobraking does the braking.
🪐 EXPLORE — An open 3D solar system with NASA-derived textures, cinematic planet fly-ins, NASA fact-sheet dossiers, a live transfer-path display, and a live humans-in-space feed.
🚀 PLAY — The mission design console: source-cited hardware from real spec sheets, real NASA astronauts as crew, a Science Traceability Matrix, JPL CML maturity badges, and a cruise simulation hit by real solar flares fetched live from NASA's DONKI API for the player's actual mission dates. Every design exports as a GMAT script for NASA's own trajectory tool — and NOVA, the built-in AI advisor, answers any question in context.
One-liner version: "ORBITFORGE lets anyone design, build, and fly a real NASA-style space mission in the browser — learning real rocketry standards from NASA open data, guided by an in-game AI, with every parameter cited on-screen."
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

ORBITFORGE is a browser game where anyone can design, build, and fly a real NASA-style space mission. It has three connected pillars. LEARN: a Rocket Builder academy walks kids through 5 steps — payload, engines, propellant, standards, launch — teaching real rocketry (the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, thrust-to-weight ≥ 1.2, staging, mass fractions) with real engine specs (Merlin 1D, RS-25, RL10), then flies full mission legs to orbit, the Moon, or Mars with a live physics animation showing stage separation and touchdown. EXPLORE: an open, free-flight 3D solar system built from NASA-derived planet textures — click any planet for a cinematic fly-in, a fact-sheet dossier, and its available missions. PLAY: a mission design console where players pick a launch vehicle, propulsion, power, communications, instruments, and even crew of real NASA astronauts, then watch live constraint gauges (Δv, mass, power, data-link duty cycle, budget) computed from source-cited specifications. When the mission launches, the cruise simulation is hit by real solar flares fetched live from NASA's DONKI API for the player's actual mission dates. An in-game AI advisor, NOVA, answers any question in the context of what's on screen.

What benefits does it have?

It turns abstract engineering trade-offs into hands-on intuition: players feel why heavier payloads shrink Δv, why solar panels fail at Jupiter but RTGs don't, why Mars landings cost less Δv than Moon landings (aerobraking!), and why "add another instrument" isn't free. Every lesson is grounded in real, cited numbers from NASA open data, so the game doubles as a classroom tool — teachers can run it with zero installation on any school laptop. It is accessible by design: browser-based, no login, no backend, and fully playable offline through graceful fallbacks when APIs are unreachable. Kids get genuine NASA engineering standards (NASA Glenn's Beginner's Guide to Rockets, CubeSat 101) instead of gamified trivia, and the built-in NOVA advisor acts like a patient mentor, answering any question in context. Advanced players even export their design as a real GMAT mission script — a bridge from game to NASA's professional trajectory tool.

What is the intended impact of the project?

We want a student's first contact with space mission design to feel like mission control, not a textbook. The intended impact is threefold: (1) Demystify the engineering design process — show kids that missions are built through iterate-fail-learn cycles against real constraints, exactly the NASA practice, and reward iteration rather than punishing failure. (2) Create a classroom-ready gateway into space STEM that runs on any device, uses only open data, and cites every source on-screen so students learn to trace claims back to NASA's actual datasets. (3) Seed long-term curiosity — by connecting gameplay to the real tools (GMAT), real data (DONKI, NeoWs), and real people (NASA astronauts as crew), we hope players graduate from our game to NASA's actual open tools and challenges. Our open-source repo lets educators worldwide adapt the catalogs and missions for their own classrooms.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Languages & frameworks: TypeScript, React 19, Vite 8, and Three.js for the 3D solar system — no game engine, no backend server; everything runs client-side in the browser. Data: NASA open APIs (api.nasa.gov: DONKI solar-weather, NeoWs asteroid feed, APOD imagery), datasets referenced from data.nasa.gov and code.nasa.gov (GMAT, CML framework, CubeSat 101, NASA Glenn rocket guides), plus the open-notify live humans-in-space feed. Design/assets: NASA-derived CC-BY planet textures (Solar System Scope). Development environment: Node.js 22, git, VS Code–style editor on a standard consumer laptop — no specialized hardware, GPUs, or cloud services required. Deployment: GitHub + GitHub Pages (free public hosting), with environment-variable configuration for API keys and graceful offline fallbacks so the demo never breaks. Documentation: the pitch deck was generated programmatically with python-pptx.

How is your project creative?

Three creative bets make ORBITFORGE stand out. (1) Real data drives real gameplay: instead of random "space events," our cruise simulation fetches actual solar flares from NASA's DONKI API for the player's actual mission dates — an X-class flare that really happened degrades your spacecraft. Even our asteroid targets are real objects passing Earth this week (NeoWs). (2) The constraint gauges are honest physics: Δv comes from the actual Tsiolkovsky equation with the player's chosen engine Isp and mass ratio; the data-link gauge models a solid-state recorder with duty-cycling like real missions (LRO/MRO); landing on Mars is genuinely cheaper in Δv than landing on the Moon because we model aerobraking. Players discover counter-intuitive engineering truths by playing, not by being told. (3) We close the loop to real NASA tooling: a one-click export generates a GMAT mission script from the player's design, and an in-game panel maps all 9 official challenge resources to the exact feature each one powers — the game is a doorway into NASA's ecosystem, not a detour from it. And NOVA makes it self-teaching: any kid can ask "why?" at any moment.

What factors did your team consider?

Accessibility first: browser-only, no install, no account, runs on low-end school laptops and offline (every API has a built-in fallback so judging can never fail). Education integrity: every gameplay number is sourced and cited on-screen — vehicle specs, instrument masses, astronaut records, NASA standards — teaching data literacy alongside rocketry. Age-appropriate scaffolding: a beginner CubeSat rideshare mission, a kid-paced Rocket Builder with Learn cards, difficulty tiers (LEO → Moon → Mars), and NOVA's plain-language answers. Real-world constraints: NASA API rate limits (own key + DEMO_KEY fallback), venue Wi-Fi failures (offline mode), and public-demo load (static hosting, no backend to crash). Accuracy vs. fun trade-offs: we simplified orbital mechanics to 1D/leg-based models but kept the equations and constants real, and we label simplifications honestly in-game. Safety & inclusivity: no accounts, no user data collected, open-source repo so others can adapt it. Judging practicality: instant public link, in-game mapping of all 9 official challenge resources, and a one-click GMAT export to prove the connection to real NASA tooling.
